summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo was adopted on 9 April 2008 and entered into force on 15 June 2008. Article 24 guarantees equality before the law and prohibits discrimination on grounds that include gender and sexual orientation, and the document treats human dignity as inviolable.

Sexual orientation has been a protected ground under the Law on Protection from Discrimination since 2004. The law was amended on 26 May 2015 and took effect in July 2015, adding gender identity. It covers employment, membership of organisations, education, provision of goods and services, social security and access to housing, and defines discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, victimisation and segregation.

Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both the constitutional prohibition and the 2015 statute remains inconsistent in practice, so the protections a visitor can cite are broader than what is reliably delivered.

The Criminal Code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity, as well as for those motivated by sexual orientation.

There is no administrative route to legal gender recognition. Wikipedia's article on LGBTQ rights in Kosovo states that a transgender person cannot legally change gender even if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery, and recognition has instead been pursued through the courts. Blert Morina filed suit in 2017 after the Civil Registration Agency rejected his request to change his name and gender on official identification documents, and requested constitutional review in July 2018. In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina ruled in his favour, permitting both the name and the sex marker on his identity documents to be changed without evidence of surgical intervention or other medical change. The Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency stated that the judgment would not be treated as precedent and that other transgender people would have to go through a similar court procedure. Reporting from January 2019 had already described legal gender recognition in Kosovo as running through the courts, with Morina's constitutional case then pending.

Article 14 of the Law on Family defines marriage as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes. A 7 July 2020 proposal for same-sex civil partnerships in a new Civil Code was rejected by the Assembly on 16 March 2022, with 28 of 120 MPs voting in favour. Prime Minister Albin Kurti announced an intent to legalise same-sex unions on 25 April 2024, and during Pride week in 2023 had said he would do his utmost to secure adoption of the Civil Code, with a Justice Ministry working group drafting the bill. As of February 2026 Parliament had still not adopted the new Civil Code, amid fierce opposition that included the ruling party.

LGBTQ people in Kosovo tend not to report discrimination or abuse to police. In 2019, 10 bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people were reported to the authorities, while a further 13 were reported only to LGBTQ organisations. In February 2019 authorities initiated a case against a Ministry of Justice official who had called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded, and police took him into custody.

CSGD, a local LGBTQI+ organisation, provides free confidential legal aid and psychological support in person and through an online application. Its services include reproductive and sexual health care with support for transgender people navigating hormonal procedures in cooperation with the Ministry, free HIV testing, and free PrEP at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since 12 June 2024.
tangentialFactors:
Consensual same-sex intercourse has been legal in independent Kosovo since 2008. The conduct was decriminalised under Ottoman rule in 1858 and for male intercourse in 1994, and in 2004 the UN administration set the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, with sexual offences made gender-neutral.

Public LGBTI organising is visible in the capital. The first Pride parade in Pristina was held in May 2016, Pride Week has run annually since 2017, and the third annual parade was accompanied by a week of exhibitions, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty. The October 2019 march through the city centre passed without incident but under multiple threats, including anonymous warnings in 2017 telling people not to attend. The 2023 Pride Week motto was 'I love you as you are!'

CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with hate speech from politicians recorded as common during the Civil Code debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024, covering 2023, documents that the 2022 parliamentary vote rejected recognition amendments for same-sex couples.

A 2015 National Democratic Institute survey of LGBTQ+ Kosovars found 81% had been subject to psychological abuse and 29% reported being victims of physical violence; a separate study by the same organisation found over 97% of respondents unwilling to accept their child if they came out as lesbian or gay. These figures are historical and cover LGBTQ+ respondents broadly rather than transgender people specifically.

A 2018 Blood Donation Week guideline bars from donation people who have 'intimate relationships with the same sex'. Lesbian, gay and bisexual personnel may serve openly in the military but may face discrimination from peers. The Center for Social Emancipation describes gay life in Kosovo as underground and mostly secretive, with one gay bar in Pristina.

Government support for LGBTI visibility has included a late 2013 parliamentary bill to create a coordinating group for the LGBTQ community, a 17 May 2014 march against homophobia attended by politicians and diplomats and welcomed by the European Union office, and a large LGBTQ flag displayed on the front of the government building that night. An IntelliNews analysis reads the new Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language as opening the way to same-sex marriage.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents have no administrative procedure for changing gender markers. Recognition is obtained only by litigating, and the December 2019 Basic Court of Pristina judgment in Blert Morina's case was expressly declared non-precedential by the Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency, so each subsequent applicant must bring a comparable case.

Residents can invoke the 2015 Anti-Discrimination Law on gender identity grounds across employment, education, goods and services, social security and housing, and can invoke the April 2019 Criminal Code's enhanced penalties where a hate crime is motivated by the victim's gender identity. Reporting practice limits both: only 10 bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people reached the authorities in 2019, against 13 reported solely to LGBTQ organisations.

CSGD operates free confidential legal aid and psychological support for residents in person and via app.csgd-ks.org, and runs reproductive and sexual health services that include help for transgender people working through hormonal procedures with the Ministry, free HIV testing, and free PrEP at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since 12 June 2024.

Residents in relationships lack statutory recognition: the Assembly rejected civil-union provisions on 16 March 2022 and the new Civil Code remained unadopted as of February 2026, so Article 14 of the Law on Family continues to define marriage as a community of two persons of different sexes.

Underreporting to police is documented as a pattern among LGBTQ residents, and the 2015 survey findings on abuse and family rejection, though now a decade old, remain the only prevalence figures in this record.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not set out the procedure, timeline or cost of the court route to gender recognition, and do not record whether the reasoning in the December 2019 Morina judgment has since been applied to any other applicant. Whether any statutory or administrative route now exists is unresolved: Wikipedia's blanket statement that legal gender change is unavailable sits alongside that judgment without reconciliation.

No source addresses non-binary or X markers, nor marker rules for passports and birth certificates beyond the identity-document case described here.

No trans-specific prevalence or violence statistics appear in this inventory. The 2015 National Democratic Institute figures cover LGBTQ+ respondents broadly and are historical; the 2019 crime counts are raw numbers with no denominator and no population comparison, so they indicate reporting behaviour rather than magnitude.

The claim that discrimination and statisation against the LGBTQ+ community remains very rampant refers to LGBTQ+ people generally. The record contains no separate sourced statement on societal attitudes toward transgender people specifically.

Nothing in the inventory covers entry or visa screening, border or airport treatment of transgender travellers, or the availability of gender-affirming care beyond CSGD's hormonal-procedure support and the PrEP provision noted above.
